opus-5.5.text:
I think we're closer than people assume on some fronts and much further than the hype suggests on others.

On the closer side, the hardware has gotten dramatically cheaper and better over the last few years. You can get reasonably capable arms, decent grippers, and good cameras for a fraction of what it used to cost. On the learning side, we've seen real progress from scaling up data collection, things like teleoperation pipelines, imitation learning, and using pretrained vision and language models as a backbone. Robots can now do tasks in a lab, folding laundry or loading a dishwasher, that would have seemed like science fiction not long ago.

The gap is reliability and generalization. A demo that works 80% of the time in one kitchen is a research result. A product has to work 99-point-something percent of the time in millions of homes that all look different: different lighting, different clutter, pets, kids, weird objects. Every failure in a home is expensive. It might break a glass, scare someone, or just be annoying enough that the robot ends up in the closet. The long tail of the home environment is brutal, and we don't yet have a clear recipe for closing it.

Then there's the business side: cost, safety certification, maintenance, and the question of what single task justifies the price. I think the first successful products will be narrow. They'll do one or two things really well, maybe with some remote human assistance in the loop for hard cases. That kind of product feels like it's a few years away. A general-purpose household robot that you just tell what to do and it handles it reliably is, in my view, still quite a bit further out, probably closer to a decade than to a year or two.

So I'm optimistic, but I'd bet on incremental, constrained products first. A Roomba-shaped wedge into the home seems more likely than a Rosie-the-robot moment.

r001.rationale: The response says narrow household robot products may be a few years away, while a general-purpose robot is closer to a decade away. It does not estimate household robotics broadly as at least five to seven years from commercial shipment.

r002.rationale: The response discusses technical reliability, cost, safety, and product scope, but does not suggest that reducing technical uncertainty would leave capital investment as the remaining push.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the guest, directly.

Honestly, I think we're further than the demos make it look, and the gap is in a boring place. The learning side has moved really fast. If you ask "can a robot pick up this mug, fold this towel, open this drawer," in a lab, with a known setup, the answer is yes, and it's gotten dramatically easier in the last two or three years with imitation learning and diffusion-style policies. You collect a few hundred demonstrations, you train, and you get something that looks magical in a video.

The problem is that a product is not a video. A product is: it works in your house, and your house is not my house. The lighting is different, the drawer sticks, the cat walks through the scene, the mug is a shape nobody in the training set had. And the failure mode for a robot isn't a bad autocomplete, it's a knocked-over glass or a scratched table, and after that happens twice the thing goes in the closet. So the bar is really high reliability, like ninety-nine point something percent on tasks people actually care about, and we are nowhere near that on open-ended household stuff. We're maybe at eighty, ninety percent on narrow things, which sounds close but is a totally different product.

The other thing people underestimate is hardware. Software people, me included, like to pretend the body is a solved problem and it's all about the policy. It's not. Getting a reasonably dexterous, safe, quiet arm plus a mobile base down to a price point where a household buys it, with enough uptime that you're not sending a technician every month, that's a manufacturing and supply chain problem, and those don't compress on a Moore's law curve. The companies that look promising to me are the ones treating hardware and data collection as the actual company, with the model as something you iterate on top.

So if I had to put a number on it, I'd say narrow household products, one or two tasks, dishes or laundry in a semi-structured setting, you'll see real shipping attempts in the next couple of years, and some of them will be genuinely useful even if they're clunky. The "general home robot that does whatever you ask" thing, I think that's still a long way out, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who tells you otherwise, mostly because the data you need for that doesn't exist yet, and nobody's figured out a cheap way to get it at the scale that language models got text.

The thing that would change my mind is if someone cracks the data flywheel, where deployed robots actually make the next model better rather than just generating support tickets. If that loop closes, the timeline shortens a lot. Until then I'd say: exciting research, premature product.

r001.rationale: It predicts narrow household products may make shipping attempts within a couple of years and says general-purpose robots are still a long way off, without estimating a five-to-seven-year timeline.

r002.rationale: It identifies data, reliability, hardware, and manufacturing challenges, but does not suggest that resolving technical uncertainty would leave capital investment as the remaining step.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by household robotics. If you mean a robot that does one fairly constrained task, we already have examples of that. If you mean a robot you can bring into your house and say, “Clean up the kitchen, do the laundry, and put everything away,” I think we’re still quite far away.

The gap is between getting something to work in a demo and getting it to work reliably in somebody’s home. Every home is different, objects are in unexpected places, and there are people and pets moving around. And when the robot fails, you can’t expect the customer to become a robotics engineer to get it going again.

So I’d expect companies to ship narrower products first, where they can control enough of the problem to make the experience useful. I’m less confident about putting a date on a general household robot. There’s still a lot to solve beyond making the robot look capable for a few minutes.

r001.rationale: The response says general-purpose household robots are “still quite far away” but gives no estimate of five to seven years or any other timeframe.

r002.rationale: It discusses reliability and technical challenges and expects narrower products first, but does not suggest that reducing technical uncertainty would leave capital investment as the remaining push.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by household robotics. If you mean a robot that does one fairly constrained task, you can build a product around that. If you mean a general-purpose robot that you can bring into somebody’s house and say, “Do the laundry, clean the kitchen, put things away,” I think we’re still quite far away.

The gap is reliability. You can get a robot to do something in a demo, but a product has to work every day, in houses you’ve never seen, with objects you’ve never seen. And when it fails, it can’t require a robotics researcher to come over and fix it. So I’m optimistic about the progress, but I wouldn’t equate an impressive demonstration with something that’s ready to ship.
